extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in media accountability, journalism professionals, and The Intercept subscribers
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic piece reporting on the New York Times' internal leak investigation and ensuing editorial controversies over Gaza coverage, including policy guidance, staff discipline, and questions about reporting accuracy. It describes actions taken, internal memos, union grievances, and the fallout for reporters and freelancers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality of the journalistic process / handling proprietary materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry was said to be 'focused narrowly on how internal materials were shared with outsiders.' Executive editor Joe Kahn emphasized the need to 'protect the confidentiality of the journalistic process' and to ensure internal materials remain internal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify gaps in how proprietary journalistic material is handled and take steps to address them. Treat sharing pre-publication and pre-broadcast materials as 'internal, confidential, and sensitive' matters that can justify formal inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leak investigations must be non-discriminatory and not single out employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York Times Guild alleged the probe singled out and discriminated against reporters of Middle Eastern and North African extraction, saying members 'faced extensive questions about their involvement in MENA ERG events and discussions' and were asked to turn over membership lists and names of colleagues who 'raised concerns' privately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should avoid targeting employees based on ethnicity, association, or membership in employee resource groups; procedures should respect privacy and avoid coercive demands for private-group information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit criticism and attacks on colleagues outside proper channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Times editorial leaders emphasized that criticism and attacks on colleagues or the journalism of the Times was prohibited 'outside of the proper channels.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff should raise concerns through designated internal channels rather than public or external forums; editorial leaders should define and communicate what constitute 'proper channels.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct standards for staff and freelancers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times reviewed a freelancer's prior social media 'likes' and described those 'likes' as 'unacceptable violations of our company policy,' leading to the paper cutting ties with the freelancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists' prior public social media activity can be judged against company policy; problematic posts/likes that predate employment may lead to review and potential termination of collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial language guidance for Gaza coverage (restrict certain terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A leaked Times style memo instructed journalists covering Israel’s war on Gaza to restrict the use of the terms 'genocide' and 'ethnic cleansing' and to 'avoid' using the phrase 'occupied territory' when describing Palestinian land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters were directed to limit use of highly charged legal/political terms and to follow internal style guidance when describing contentious events and territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous reporting, editing, and verification of witness accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times public defense noted that reporters 'were part of a rigorous reporting and editing process.' The article documents cases where anonymous witness accounts were later undermined by video and other reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic standards call for cross-checking eyewitness accounts, seeking corroborating evidence (e.g., video, multiple sources), and being cautious with anonymous sources; relying on single unverified accounts is an anti-pattern that can produce serious errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction and update practices — transparency when reporting is undermined
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of issuing a full correction, the Times inserted a bracketed 'update' within the body of the story when parts of the December 28 article were undermined, noting that an entire section was incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should clearly correct or retract erroneous reporting rather than only adding buried updates; transparent correction practices help maintain accountability and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguarding internal communication channels and appropriate handling of membership/participant lists
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the probe, group leaders were asked to turn over the MENA ERG membership list and names of colleagues who had raised private concerns; a reporter was removed from a WhatsApp group used for Gaza coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal messaging groups and ERG memberships should be protected from being used as investigatory leads without clear, justified processes; removal from communication channels and demands for private lists raise procedural and privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution, credit, and institutional accountability when reporting errors occur
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times sought to 'stand behind' its reporting while also later seeking to share credit for reporting that was shown to have serious problems; the Polk committee stood by its citation even as internal questions arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should clearly explain the basis for contested assertions, be transparent about who contributed to reporting, and address how awards or credit relate to later-discovered errors to maintain institutional accountability.
